skills.name: Prepare the sulphides of sodium and iron and describe their properties

note.text:
A sulphide is a compound of a metal with sulphur.
Iron(II) sulphide: heat a mixture of iron filings and sulphur. Fe + S → FeS. The mixture glows and goes on reacting without more heating, because the reaction gives out heat. The product is a black solid.
Sodium sulphide: made by heating sodium with sulphur, or by reducing sodium sulphate with carbon. It is a solid that dissolves easily in water to give an alkaline solution.
A compound is not a mixture: a magnet picks iron out of a MIXTURE of iron and sulphur, but not out of FeS; the mixture shows yellow specks, while FeS is uniformly black.
Both sulphides give hydrogen sulphide with a dilute acid: FeS + 2HCl → FeCl2 + H2S.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to prepare the sulphides of iron and sodium, tell a compound from a mixture, and work out the masses that combine.
Builds on: Lesson {6} (hydrogen sulphide) and Form One compounds and mixtures.
Leads to: Lesson {8} (sulphuric acid) and the mole calculations of the third chapter.

sections.heading: Making the sulphides
sections.text:
Iron(II) sulphide: mix iron filings with powdered sulphur and heat one spot strongly. The mixture begins to glow red and goes on reacting without further heating, because the reaction gives out heat:
Fe + S → {formula('FeS')}
The product is a black solid.
Sodium sulphide: made by heating sodium with sulphur, or in industry by reducing sodium sulphate with carbon. It is a solid that dissolves readily in water, giving an alkaline solution.
Both sulphides give hydrogen sulphide with a dilute acid, which is how the gas is prepared.

sections.heading: Compound against mixture

key_words.meaning: a compound of a metal with sulphur
substances together but not chemically joined
giving out heat, as the iron and sulphur reaction does
the fixed ratio by mass in which elements combine in a compound

examples: {56} g of Fe needs {32} g of S

mistake.wrong: a magnet separates iron from iron(II) sulphide
mistake.right: a magnet separates iron from a MIXTURE of iron and sulphur only
mistake.why: In the compound the iron is chemically joined and the solid is not magnetic.

worked_example.problem: Give two ways of showing that the black solid made by heating iron and sulphur is a compound, not a mixture.
steps: Hold a magnet near it: a mixture gives up its iron filings to the magnet, but the compound does not.
Look at it closely: a mixture shows yellow specks of sulphur among grey iron, but the compound is uniformly black.
Add dilute hydrochloric acid: the mixture gives hydrogen (odourless), the compound gives hydrogen sulphide (rotten eggs).
In a compound the elements have lost their own properties.
worked_example.answer: a magnet no longer picks out iron, and the solid is uniformly black

pick.q: How is iron(II) sulphide prepared in the laboratory?
pick.r: By heating a mixture of iron filings and sulphur
w: By adding iron filings to dilute sulphuric acid
By adding iron filings to water containing sulphur
e: Iron with dilute sulphuric acid gives iron(II) sulphate and hydrogen.
Burning iron in air gives an oxide, not a sulphide.
Sulphur is insoluble in water, and no reaction takes place in the cold.
pick.y: Fe + S → {formula('FeS')}: once started, the mixture glows and keeps reacting by itself.

pick.q: What is seen when a mixture of iron filings and sulphur is heated strongly?
pick.r: The mixture glows red and keeps reacting without more heating
w: The mixture melts and runs like a liquid
A brown gas is given off
Nothing happens until acid is added
e: The product is a solid that does not melt at that temperature.
No brown gas is formed; the product is a black solid.
The reaction starts with heat alone.
pick.y: The reaction gives out heat, so it continues on its own once it has started.

pick.q: How can iron(II) sulphide be told from a mixture of iron and sulphur?
pick.r: A magnet picks iron out of the mixture but not out of the compound
w: The compound is yellow and the mixture is black
Both behave in exactly the same way
Only the compound can be seen with a hand lens
e: It is the other way round in colour terms: the compound is black and the mixture shows yellow specks.
A compound has properties of its own, different from those of its elements.
Both can be seen; the difference is in their properties.
pick.y: In a mixture the elements keep their own properties, so the iron is still magnetic.

pick.q: What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to iron(II) sulphide?
e: Hydrogen comes from a metal with an acid, not from a sulphide.
Sulphur dioxide comes from a sulphite with an acid.
The reaction is the standard way of making {formula('H2S')}.

pick.q: Which statement about sodium sulphide is correct?
pick.r: It is soluble in water and its solution is alkaline
e: Sodium compounds are generally soluble, and sodium sulphide is no exception.
The solution of a salt of a strong base and a weak acid is alkaline, not acidic.
It is a solid, not a gas.
pick.y: {formula('Na2S')} dissolves and its solution is alkaline because the sulphide ion reacts with water.

pick.q: Why is iron(II) sulphide used, rather than sodium sulphide, to make hydrogen sulphide in the laboratory?
pick.r: It is a solid that reacts steadily with dilute acid, so the flow of gas is easy to control
w: Sodium sulphide gives a different gas
Iron(II) sulphide is the only sulphide that exists
Sodium sulphide does not react with acids
e: Both give hydrogen sulphide with an acid.
Many metal sulphides exist, such as {formula('Na2S')}, {formula('ZnS')} and {formula('PbS')}.
Sodium sulphide does react, and very readily.
pick.y: Lumps of {formula('FeS')} react at a steady rate, while the very soluble {formula('Na2S')} would react too fast.

pick.w1: A magnet picks iron out of both
pick.w2: A magnet picks iron out of the compound only
pick.w3: A magnet has no effect on either
pick.y: In a mixture each element keeps its own properties, so the iron is still magnetic.

pick.r: The mixture shows yellow specks among grey, while the compound is uniformly black

pick.r: The mixture gives an odourless gas, the compound a gas smelling of rotten eggs

questions.prompt: How can you tell iron(II) sulphide from a mixture of iron and sulphur by {M.q}?
What mass of sulphur, in grams, combines exactly with {m} g of iron to make iron(II) sulphide?

misconceptions.explain: Equal moles do not mean equal masses: iron and sulphur have different relative atomic masses.
Divide by the relative atomic mass of IRON and multiply by that of sulphur.

solution: Fe + S → {formula('FeS')}: {1} mol of iron needs {1} mol of sulphur.
{m} g of iron is {m} ÷ {ram('Fe')} = {roundTo(m / ram('Fe'), 0.001)} mol.
That needs the same number of moles of sulphur: {roundTo(m / ram('Fe'), 0.001)} × {ram('S')} = {answer} g.

questions.prompt: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to {C.n}. What gas is given off?
What mass of iron(II) sulphide, in grams, is made when {m} g of iron combines completely with sulphur?

misconceptions.explain: The sulphur adds to the mass: the product is heavier than the iron alone.
That is the mass of SULPHUR needed; the question asks for the mass of {formula('FeS')}.

solution: {m} g of iron is {roundTo(m / ram('Fe'), 0.001)} mol.
Fe + S → {formula('FeS')}, so the same number of moles of {formula('FeS')} is made.
The relative formula mass of {formula('FeS')} is {molarMass('FeS')}, so the mass is {roundTo(m / ram('Fe'), 0.001)} × {molarMass('FeS')} = {answer} g.
